name: Chan (Chinese Meditation school)
alt_names: Foxin zong 佛心宗 (school of the buddha-mind)
regions: China (Song-shan, Huangmei, Caoxi, Jiangxi, Hunan, Zhejiang, Fujian, Sichuan)

tradition.text: from Bodhidharma's arrival in China (traditionally 520 or 527 CE); transmitted from Śākyamuni through 28 Indian patriarchs

scholarly.text: a self-conscious lineage from the late 7th c. (East Mountain, Northern school); classical Tang Chan 8th–10th c.; dominant public Buddhism of the Song (960–1279); living

transmissions_received.what: Laṅkāvatāra, Prajñāpāramitā (Diamond Sūtra), Vimalakīrti, Nirvāṇa-sūtra buddha-nature teaching, Awakening of Faith
transmissions_received.evidence: Bodhidharma's gift of the four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra to Huike (Xu gaoseng zhuan, T2060 juan 16); Huineng's awakening on the Diamond Sūtra (Platform Sūtra)

transmissions_given.what: Chan lineages and practice (Nine Mountain schools, from the 9th c.)
Linji (Huanglong, Yangqi), Caodong and Ming Linji (Ōbaku) transmissions to Japan
Chan lineages in Vietnam (Thiền), culminating in the Trúc Lâm school (U55)

distinctive_positions: A 'separate transmission outside the teachings, not dependent on words and letters, pointing directly at the human mind: see the nature and become a buddha' (the tradition's four-line self-description, assembled by the Song).
The mind (xin 心) or self-nature (zixing 自性) is originally pure and complete; delusion and awakening differ, the nature does not (Platform Sūtra).
Transmission from mind to mind (yi xin chuan xin 以心傳心) through a line of patriarchs, authenticated by a living teacher.
Samādhi and prajñā are one in substance (lamp and light); no-thought is the tenet, no-form the substance, non-abiding the root (Platform Sūtra).
Sudden awakening (dunwu 頓悟) is upheld against 'gradual' views; the relation of awakening to cultivation is debated within Chan itself.
Encounter dialogue, shouts and blows, and later public cases (gong'an) and the critical phrase (huatou) as means of awakening.
Monastic life organised by the 'pure rules' (qinggui) with communal work (puqing) as practice.
summary: The Chinese school of the 'meditation' (chan 禪, from dhyāna) lineage, which traces itself through 28 Indian patriarchs to Bodhidharma and six Chinese patriarchs ending with Huineng, divides into the Northern and Southern schools and later the Five Houses, and teaches seeing one's own nature as buddha through direct pointing, sitting meditation, encounter dialogue and kōan practice.

name: Seon (Korean Chan)

tradition.text: Beomnang is said to have received Chan from the Fourth Patriarch Daoxin (7th c.); Doui returned from Tang China in 821 with Hongzhou transmission

scholarly.text: from the 9th c. (Nine Mountain schools); Goryeo synthesis (Jinul, 12th–13th c.); Joseon suppression and survival; modern Jogye Order (1962)

transmissions_received.what: Mazu's Hongzhou lineage via Xitang Zhizang and others (Doui, Hongcheok, Hyecheol)
Yangqi-Linji transmission to Taego Bou and Naong Hyegeun (14th c.)
Huayan (Hwaeom) doctrine integrated by Jinul through Li Tongxuan and Zongmi

distinctive_positions: Sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation (dono jeomsu 頓悟漸修) as the normative path (Jinul).
The mind as 'empty and calm, numinous awareness' (gongjeok yeongji 空寂靈知) to be recognised by tracing back the radiance (Jinul, after Zongmi).
Harmony of Seon and the doctrinal teachings (seon-gyo ilchi), yet the hwadu 'shortcut' is the highest gate (Jinul, Hyujeong).
Ganhwa Seon (observing the critical phrase) as the mainstream practice of the Jogye order.
In the 20th c. Seongcheol argued for sudden awakening/sudden cultivation (dono donsu) against Jinul (see dsp:seon-sudden-cultivation-debate).
summary: Korean Chan: introduced from Tang China from the 9th century as the Nine Mountain schools, unified in doctrine and practice by Jinul (1158–1210) around sudden awakening/gradual cultivation and hwadu practice, and carried on by Taego, Hyujeong and the modern Jogye Order.

name: Zen (Japanese Chan)
regions: Japan (Kamakura, Kyoto, Echizen, Noto, Suruga, Uji)

tradition.text: Rinzai from Eisai's return in 1191; Sōtō from Dōgen's return in 1227; Ōbaku from Ingen's arrival in 1654

scholarly.text: earlier contacts (Dōshō 7th c., Yixuan/Gikū 9th c., Kakua 12th c.); Kamakura foundations 12th–13th c.; Five Mountains system 14th c.; Tokugawa reforms 17th–18th c.; living

transmissions_received.what: Huanglong- and Yangqi-branch Linji lineages (Eisai; Enni; émigré Chinese masters)
Caodong lineage from Tiantong Rujing to Dōgen

distinctive_positions: Zazen as the heart of practice, understood by Sōtō as just sitting (shikantaza) in which practice and realization are one, and by Rinzai as the field of kōan introspection leading to kenshō.
Transmission certified face to face (menju) with documents of succession (shisho, inka).
Monastic rule adapted from the Chinese qinggui; work, ritual and daily conduct as practice.
summary: Japanese Chan: the Rinzai, Sōtō and Ōbaku lineages established from the late 12th to the 17th century, teaching seated meditation (zazen), kōan introspection or just sitting, and monastic life as the direct realization of buddha-nature.

name: Rinzai Zen

scholarly.text: Kamakura and Muromachi Five Mountains (gozan) and the rinka lines; all present-day Rinzai lines descend through Hakuin (18th c.) from the Ōtōkan line (Nanpo–Daitō–Kanzan)

transmissions_received.what: Linji house lineages (Huanglong via Eisai; Yangqi via Enni, Lanxi, Wuxue, Nanpo's master Xutang)

distinctive_positions: Kōan introspection under a teacher in private interview (sanzen/dokusan) as the path to kenshō.
Great doubt (daigi), great faith and great determination as the three essentials of practice.
Post-kenshō training (gogo no shugyō) through a graded kōan curriculum systematised in Hakuin's line.
Hakuin's teaching that seeing the nature must issue in the 'four wisdoms' and compassionate activity.
summary: The Japanese form of the Linji house: introduced by Eisai and Chinese émigré masters in the Kamakura period, patronised through the Five Mountains, revived in the 18th century by Hakuin, whose kōan system all living Rinzai lines follow.

name: Sōtō Zen

tradition.text: from Dōgen's transmission from Tiantong Rujing (1225) and return (1227)

scholarly.text: founded 13th c.; spread widely among provincial laity from Keizan onward; Tokugawa sectarian reforms (Manzan, Menzan); living

transmissions_received.what: Caodong lineage (Furong Daokai → … → Tiantong Rujing → Dōgen)
former Daruma-shū monks (Ejō, Gikai, Giin, Gien) joined Dōgen's community

distinctive_positions: Just sitting (shikantaza) as the whole of practice, not a means to a later awakening.
Oneness of practice and realization (shushō ittō): sitting is itself the enactment of buddhahood.
Dropping off body and mind (shinjin datsuraku) as Dōgen's account of his awakening under Rujing.
Being-time (uji), impermanence as buddha-nature (mujō busshō), and the whole world as the 'kōan realized' (genjōkōan).
Deep faith in cause and effect (jinshin inga) against readings that deny karma after awakening.
summary: The Japanese Caodong lineage founded by Dōgen (1200–1253) after training with Tiantong Rujing, centred on just sitting as the enactment of original awakening, expanded by Keizan (1268–1325) into Japan's largest Zen denomination.

name: Ōbaku Zen

tradition.text: from Ingen Ryūki's arrival in Nagasaki (1654) and the founding of Ōbakusan Manpukuji (1661)

scholarly.text: 17th c. Ming-dynasty Linji transmission; living

transmissions_received.what: Ming Linji lineage of Miyun Yuanwu and Feiyin Tongrong at Wanfusi, Mount Huangbo (Fujian)

distinctive_positions: Ming-style monastic observance: Chinese-pronounced sūtra chanting, Ming precepts platform and rules (Ōbaku shingi).
Combination of kōan meditation with recitation of Amitābha's name (nenbutsu Zen), which Hakuin's Rinzai line criticised.
Printing of the complete canon (Tetsugen edition) as Dharma work.
summary: The third Japanese Zen denomination, founded by the Chinese Linji master Yinyuan Longqi (Ingen, 1592–1673), which preserves Ming Chinese monastic forms and combines Zen with Pure Land recitation.

name: Linji house

scholarly.text: 9th-c. origin; dominant Chan house from the Song onward; living in Chinese Chan

transmissions_given.what: Yangqi line via Shiwu Qinggong / Pingshan Chulin to Taego and Naong

distinctive_positions: The true person of no rank (wuwei zhenren) and the 'person of the Way who depends on nothing' (wuyi daoren) listening to the Dharma here and now.
Shouts (he 喝) and blows as means; the four classifications (siliaojian), four guest-host relations, four illumination-function relations, three mysteries and three essentials.
'Be master wherever you are; wherever you stand is true'; nothing to do (wushi 無事).
In the Song, kōan commentary (Yuanwu) and the critical phrase (Dahui's kanhua Chan).
summary: One of the Five Houses of Chan, stemming from Linji Yixuan (d. 866) in the line of Mazu and Huangbo, known for its shouts and devices; through its Yangqi branch it became the main Chinese Chan lineage and the source of Japanese Rinzai and Ōbaku.

name: Caodong house

tradition.text: founded by Dongshan Liangjie (807–869) and Caoshan Benji (840–901)

scholarly.text: 9th c.; nearly extinct in the 10th c.; revived in the Northern Song by Touzi Yiqing; living

transmissions_given.what: Rujing's line to Dōgen (and Dongming Huiri's line to Tōmyō Enichi)

distinctive_positions: The five ranks of the real and the apparent (zheng-pian wuwei) and the five ranks of merit.
Mutual interfusion and non-interfusion (huihu 回互) of principle and phenomena (Cantongqi).
Silent illumination (mozhao) as the Song Caodong practice (Hongzhi).
'Precious Mirror Samādhi' (Baojing sanmei): the reflection and the one reflected.
summary: One of the Five Houses of Chan, named from Dongshan Liangjie and Caoshan Benji in the line of Qingyuan and Shitou, known for the five ranks and later for Hongzhi's silent illumination; source of Japanese Sōtō.

name: Yunmen house

scholarly.text: 10th c.; flourishing in the Northern Song; absorbed by the Linji house in the Southern Song

distinctive_positions: One-word barriers (yizi guan 一字關) and terse replies.
Yunmen's three phrases as systematised by Deshan Yuanmi: containing heaven and earth, cutting off the myriad streams, following the waves.
'Every day is a good day' (Biyan lu case 6).
summary: One of the Five Houses of Chan, from Yunmen Wenyan (864–949) in Xuefeng's line; famed for single-word responses, it produced Xuedou Chongxian, whose verses on a hundred cases became the Blue Cliff Record.

name: Guiyang house

tradition.text: founded by Guishan Lingyou (771–853) and Yangshan Huiji (807–883)

scholarly.text: 9th c.; the first of the Five Houses to die out (by the late 10th c.)

distinctive_positions: Circle-figures (yuanxiang 圓相) as a teaching device, said to come from Nanyang Huizhong through Danyuan (Rentian yanmu).
Sudden awakening to principle with gradual removal of habit energies (Guishan).
summary: The earliest of the Five Houses, from Guishan Lingyou and his heir Yangshan Huiji in the line of Baizhang; known for the harmony of master and disciple and for circle-figures, it disappeared as a distinct line by the Song.

name: Fayan house

scholarly.text: 10th c.; faded in the Song (11th c.)

transmissions_given.what: Goryeo monks trained under Yongming Yanshou (tradition says 36)

distinctive_positions: Use of Huayan categories (the six characteristics) within Chan (Rentian yanmu).
'Not knowing is most intimate' (Luohan Guichen to Fayan).
Harmony of Chan with the scriptural teachings and with Pure Land practice (Yongming Yanshou).
summary: The last of the Five Houses to form, from Fayan Wenyi (885–958) in the line of Xuansha and Luohan Guichen; it drew on Huayan doctrine, produced Yongming Yanshou's synthesis of Chan and the teachings, and faded by the 11th century.

name: East Mountain teaching
regions: Huangmei (Hubei), Mount Shuangfeng and East Mountain

scholarly.text: c. 624–674 (Daoxin and Hongren's communities)

distinctive_positions: Guarding the one (shouyi 守一) and 'one-practice samādhi' (Daoxin).
Guarding the original true mind (shou benzhen xin 守本真心) (Hongren).
Large settled communities combining meditation and labour.
summary: The communities of the Fourth and Fifth Patriarchs Daoxin and Hongren at Huangmei, from which both the Northern school and Huineng's line claimed descent.

name: Northern school of Chan

scholarly.text: c. 700–c. 800 (imperial favour 701–730s; declined after Shenhui's attacks and the An Lushan rebellion)

distinctive_positions: Contemplating the mind (guanxin) and 'viewing purity' (kanjing).
The five expedient means (wu fangbian) of the Dasheng wusheng fangbian men.
The mind is originally pure but obscured by adventitious dust; practice removes it (the view the Platform Sūtra ascribes to Shenxiu's verse).
summary: The metropolitan Chan of Shenxiu (d. 706) and his heirs Puji and Yifu, favoured by the Tang court; Shenhui attacked it in 730–732 as collateral and gradual, a characterization later Chan histories adopted.

name: Heze school
distinctive_positions: Sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation (as later summarised by Zongmi).
Knowing (zhi 知) — 'the one word knowing is the gate of all wonders' — as the substance of mind (Zongmi's report of Heze teaching).
No-thought (wunian) as the tenet; Huineng as the true Sixth Patriarch.
summary: The line of Heze Shenhui (684–758), who championed Huineng and sudden awakening; Zongmi counted himself its heir and systematised its teaching of numinous knowing.

name: Oxhead school

tradition.text: founded by Farong (594–657), said to have been instructed by the Fourth Patriarch Daoxin

scholarly.text: the lineage is attested from the 8th c.; the link to Daoxin is regarded by scholars as a later construction

distinctive_positions: The Way is fundamentally empty; 'forgetting feelings' (wangqing) rather than guarding mind (Zongmi's report).
Insentient things possess the Way (Jueguan lun, as generally described).
summary: A Tang Chan lineage of the Jiangnan region traced to Niutou Farong, which stressed emptiness and non-attachment and was classed by Zongmi as the school that 'eliminates traces'.

name: Jingzhong school

scholarly.text: 8th c.

distinctive_positions: Musang's three phrases: no remembering (wuyi) = precepts, no thinking (wunian) = samādhi, no forgetting/no delusion (mowang) = wisdom (Lidai fabao ji).
Mass ordination-and-teaching assemblies opened with drawn-out recitation of the Buddha's name (Lidai fabao ji).
summary: The Sichuan lineage of Zhishen, Chuji and the Korean master Musang (Kim heshang, 684–762), known from the Lidai fabao ji.

name: Baotang school

scholarly.text: later 8th c.

distinctive_positions: No-thought alone; rejection of ritual, recitation and conventional observances (Lidai fabao ji; Zongmi's criticism).
Claim that Bodhidharma's robe passed from Huineng via Empress Wu to Zhishen and on to Wuzhu (Lidai fabao ji).
summary: The radical Sichuan community of Wuzhu (714–774), which rejected all formal practice in favour of no-thought and claimed the patriarchal robe; its record is the Dunhuang Lidai fabao ji.

name: Hongzhou school

scholarly.text: later 8th–9th c.; its heirs formed the Linji and Guiyang houses

distinctive_positions: 'This very mind is buddha' and 'neither mind nor buddha' (Mazu).
'The ordinary mind is the Way'; all activity is the function of buddha-nature.
Encounter dialogue: shouts, blows and everyday gestures as direct pointing.
summary: The school of Mazu Daoyi (709–788) in Jiangxi, which taught that the ordinary functioning mind is buddha and developed encounter dialogue; its heirs Baizhang, Huangbo, Linji, Guishan and Zhaozhou shaped classical Chan.

name: Yangqi branch (of the Linji house)
regions: China; transmitted to Japan and Korea

scholarly.text: from Yangqi Fanghui (992–1049); the main Linji line from the 12th c.

transmissions_given.what: most Japanese Rinzai lines (via Wuzhun Shifan, Xutang Zhiyu, Lanxi Daolong, etc.)

distinctive_positions: Kōan commentary (Yuanwu) and the critical-phrase practice (Dahui).
summary: The branch of the Linji house descending from Yangqi Fanghui, which produced Wuzu Fayan, Yuanwu Keqin and Dahui Zonggao and became the principal source of later Chinese, Korean and Japanese Rinzai lineages.

name: Huanglong branch (of the Linji house)

scholarly.text: from Huanglong Huinan (1002–1069); faded in the 13th c.

distinctive_positions: Huanglong's 'three barriers' (Buddha's hand, donkey's leg, one's birth-conditions).
Lettered Chan (wenzi Chan) of Juefan Huihong.
summary: The branch of the Linji house from Huanglong Huinan, prominent in the Northern Song and the source of Eisai's Rinzai transmission.

name: Daruma school (Japan)

scholarly.text: late 12th c.; proscribed 1194 together with Eisai's movement; its members joined Dōgen's community in the 1240s

transmissions_received.what: Nōnin sent disciples to China (1189) who obtained a certificate from Zhuoan Deguang, an heir of Dahui

distinctive_positions: Awakening without a teacher (mushi dokugo); criticised by Eisai for rejecting precepts and practice (Kōzen gokoku ron).
summary: The first independent Zen movement in Japan, founded by Dainichi Nōnin, whose certificate came by proxy from Dahui's disciple Zhuoan Deguang; its monks later became leading disciples of Dōgen.

name: Fuke school

tradition.text: traced to Puhua, Linji's eccentric companion, and brought to Japan by Shinchi Kakushin (13th c.)

scholarly.text: organised as a Rinzai-affiliated order of mendicant shakuhachi players (komusō) in the Edo period; abolished 1871; revived by lay players

distinctive_positions: Blowing the bamboo flute (suizen 吹禪) as meditation.
summary: A Japanese order of mendicant flute-playing monks (komusō) that traced itself to the Tang eccentric Puhua; its origin legend is regarded by scholars as late.

name: Jogye order

tradition.text: the name recalls Caoxi (Jogye), Huineng's mountain; Jinul's Suseonsa community (Songgwangsa) is taken as its heartland; the modern order counts Doui as founder and Taego as reviver

scholarly.text: a Goryeo Jogye school existed from the 12th c.; the modern Jogye Order was constituted in 1962

distinctive_positions: Ganhwa Seon combined with doctrinal study (the four-text curriculum, sajip).
summary: The Korean Seon order named after Huineng's Caoxi, which regards Jinul and Taego as its great masters; today the largest order of Korean Buddhism.

name: Nine Mountain Seon schools

scholarly.text: 9th–10th c.

distinctive_positions: Mostly Hongzhou-line transmissions from Mazu's heirs (Xitang Zhizang, Magu Baoche, Nanquan); one (Sumisan) from the Caodong line.
summary: The nine Seon monastic lineages founded in late Silla and early Goryeo by monks returning from Tang China, the roots of all later Korean Seon.
